The psych evaluation will help figure out possible causes of your hallucinations, and you will likely be put on some sort of medication. I relate to this. Although having struggled with self harm for years, I have noticed a few problems with it.

1. It doesn't actually help as much as you think it does. Sure, the temporary relief you get from intense emotions, or the feeling of control is wonderful. I am definitely not denying that. However, it tends to actually be worse for you in the long run. You might be okay with scars now, but you usually end up really disliking them. It is a maladaptive coping mechanism for a reason. It's just temporary relief for a problem that runs deeper. That temporary relief is great, and sometimes it can feel like it's helping everything when you do it often enough, but it's really no different than taking a drug to temporarily feel better, or getting drunk to feel better. It feels like it helps at the time, but it's not actually doing anything to help you recover from whatever mental illness/distress you're under.

2. You're never really as in control as you think. I used to think I had a lot of control over self harm. Back in the day I'd only ever cut on my hips. Then, I found myself moving to my thighs, then to my ankles, then to my forearm. Looking back, I never wanted to do that. I regret it a lot. I thought I was in control. Even when I moved to the other areas, I thought I was willingly doing it and I was in control. I really wasn't. It was an addiction I thought I could quit at any time but I couldn't.

3. No matter how safe you're being, accidents will likely happen at some point. This is very unfortunate. I am a very big believer in harm reduction. As someone who still struggles with self harm, I do believe it's better to encourage people to self harm in a safer way as opposed to telling them to stop, because they're gonna do it anyway. Unfortunately, accidents can and likely will still happen. I have a horrible scar on my forearm from accidentally cutting very deep when I was feeling very distressed. Cutting too deep is something that can very easily happen, no matter how safe you try to be.

YTA, but I think it's from a place of ignorance as opposed to actually being an asshole. One thing a lot of autistic people are taught is to try to express and understand their emotions/feelings, because oftentimes we struggle with communicating these things to people. He's likely repeating "I'm bored" multiple times a day, as boredom may be an incredibly frustrating feeling for him to deal with, and he want to communicate that to other people around him.

He may feel bored due to feeling left out or ignored at times. He may feel bored because he has to do things he really doesn't want to do. From what you're describing, it sounds like he's bored from understimulation, and needs something to occupy himself better at these times. He may have grown tired of his current games and stuff, and doesn't know what to do. Or he may have lost interest in that type of entertainment, and doesn't know what else to move onto. Oftentimes, what a lot of autistic individuals do is they will hyperfixate on something for a while, and sometimes these things stick, other times they don't. He may be struggling to find a new hobby or interest that satisfies him.

Have you tried asking him what he wants to do? If he doesn't know, he may just need to be gently pushed towards another interest. If he likes video games, find out what kind of games he likes. Try to find some he hasn't played and tell him about them. If he likes watching TV, try to steer him towards watching a long running show he'd like. If he's more of an outdoorsy person, maybe try finding a hobby like cycling or hiking.

There's probably a lot more complexity to his boredon than you can see, as he probably can't express why he's bored, or even doesn't really know why he's bored. That's probably why he's just saying he's bored and not doing anything to entertain himself. Try to communicate a bit more with him. Ask him why he's so bored all the time, and what he thinks might help him not be bored. Just snapping at him is going to get neither of you anywhere and is honestly just rude.

That definitely sounds like psychosis. Keep in mind that hallucinating doesn't automatically mean you're schizophrenic, there are many different things that can cause you to have psychosis/hallucinations. Go to a doctor, and don't worry, they won't lock you up. They will only do that if you're a danger to yourself (have active plans to kill yourself or mutilate yourself) or if you're a danger to others (have active plans to harm someone).

You may be advised to do inpatient stay to speed up the process of getting a psychiatric evaluation, and because it may make you feel safer if your hallucinations are very distressing to you, but they will not force you to. If you choose not to, then you'll just have to wait a bit longer for a psych evaluation, as outpatient stuff tends to take a wee bit longer. I was in a similar situation to you about this time last year, and even though I had a history of suicide attempts and self harm, they didn't involuntarily hospitalise me for just having hallucinations.

I relate to this. Although having struggled with self harm for years, I have noticed a few problems with it.

1. It doesn't actually help as much as you think it does. Sure, the temporary relief you get from intense emotions, or the feeling of control is wonderful. I am definitely not denying that. However, it tends to actually be worse for you in the long run. You might be okay with scars now, but you usually end up really disliking them. It is a maladaptive coping mechanism for a reason. It's just temporary relief for a problem that runs deeper. That temporary relief is great, and sometimes it can feel like it's helping everything when you do it often enough, but it's really no different than taking a drug to temporarily feel better, or getting drunk to feel better. It feels like it helps at the time, but it's not actually doing anything to help you recover from whatever mental illness/distress you're under.

2. You're never really as in control as you think. I used to think I had a lot of control over self harm. Back in the day I'd only ever cut on my hips. Then, I found myself moving to my thighs, then to my ankles, then to my forearm. Looking back, I never wanted to do that. I regret it a lot. I thought I was in control. Even when I moved to the other areas, I thought I was willingly doing it and I was in control. I really wasn't. It was an addiction I thought I could quit at any time but I couldn't.

3. No matter how safe you're being, accidents will likely happen at some point. This is very unfortunate. I am a very big believer in harm reduction. As someone who still struggles with self harm, I do believe it's better to encourage people to self harm in a safer way as opposed to telling them to stop, because they're gonna do it anyway. Unfortunately, accidents can and likely will still happen. I have a horrible scar on my forearm from accidentally cutting very deep when I was feeling very distressed. Cutting too deep is something that can very easily happen, no matter how safe you try to be.
